body: Croatian licence plates are long and white. Some have a blue EU strip, while older ones are fully white, which is common in Generation 3 coverage.
Croatian bollards are white and triangle-shaped from the top, with a black rectangle and a red or white reflector. They have sharper edges than similar bollards in Hungary and Lithuania.
The Croatian language is a Slavic language written in the Latin alphabet. The presence of 'IJE' letter combinations is a good clue to distinguish it from Serbian.
Croatian chevrons feature a red arrow on a yellow or white background.
Croatia uses square (B-type) guardrails, which is uncommon in Europe.
In Generation 3, the Google car often has a distinct blur where the side mirrors are visible. A small circular yellow sticker on the mirror is a unique clue for Croatia.
A large portion of Generation 3 coverage was filmed in autumn, resulting in distinct fall colors. This "fall vibe" is not present in Generation 4.
Older cars may have an oval 'HR' sticker, which stands for Hrvatska, the country's name in Croatian.
Croatian directional signs have a yellow background with a black outline and often a pencil-shaped tip. This design is shared with other former Yugoslav countries.
Utility poles are often cylindrical concrete or wood. Wooden poles sometimes have alternating hooks, similar to those in Latvia.
Exposed red brick walls are a feature of inland Croatian architecture. This style can also be seen in Slovenia and Serbia.
Croatia has distinctive blue fire hydrants with two diagonal protrusions. Newer versions have a smaller top but retain the blue color.
The Croatian pedestrian sign shows a person wearing a belt on a zebra crossing with 5 stripes. The belt helps distinguish it from the Slovenian sign.
Look for advertisements for the beer brands Karlovačko and Ožujsko. The supermarkets Konzum and Plodine are also exclusive to Croatia.
Croatia has no Generation 2 car coverage, but some historic areas have Generation 2 trekker coverage. Sometimes the operator's red cap is visible.
Croatian landline phone numbers usually start with a zero followed by the area code.
The northeastern part of Croatia is very flat and agricultural, resembling the landscapes of Hungary and northwestern Serbia.
The area north and west of Zagreb is characterized by hilly agricultural land.
The Adriatic coast is defined by rocky mountains, shrubbery instead of trees, and numerous islands. The landscape is similar to Montenegro and Albania.
Along the Adriatic coast, houses are often made of beige brick and commonly feature green shutters. This style is also found in parts of Italy.
The northwestern region of Istria can be identified by its distinctive red soil.
Bilingual street signs in Croatian and Italian are a strong clue for the region of Istria.
Town names ending in -ec are common in the northern part of central Croatia.
Zagreb, the capital, has a big-city feel with many apartment blocks and distinctive blue trams. The northern part of the city is hilly.
Zagreb and Osijek are the only two cities in Croatia that have trams.
The area northeast of Zadar is flat, with a distinct mountain ridge visible to the north.
The highest concentration of vineyards is found around the town of Ilok, near the Serbian border.
The city of Rijeka has unique traffic lights held up by long, blue poles that extend over the road.
In the town of Petrinja, you may see many ruined and damaged buildings due to a 2020 earthquake.
The southern city of Dubrovnik is famous for its well-preserved medieval city walls.
Tall cypress trees are a common sight near the southern tip of Croatia.
